title: You Can Leave the World Behind and Still Bring Your Self-Righteousness Into the Church
paragraphs: You Can Leave the World Behind and Still Bring Your Self-Righteousness Into the Church

You can stop drinking, stop partying, clean up your language, carry a Bible, serve in church, give faithfully, pray every morning—and still walk into the presence of God carrying something more dangerous than the sins you left behind: confidence in your own righteousness.
There is a frightening kind of lostness that does not look lost.
It knows the songs.
It knows when to raise its hands.
It knows the verses.
It knows Christian vocabulary.
It can recognize false doctrine, rebuke compromise, defend biblical morality, and tell you exactly what is wrong with the culture.
It may have a testimony about everything it no longer does.
And somewhere along the road from scandal to respectability, it can quietly begin looking at broken people and thinking:
Thank God I’m not like them.
That sentence should make every serious Christian uncomfortable.
Because Jesus once told a story about two men who entered the same place of worship.
One looked righteous.
The other knew he wasn't.
And according to Jesus, only one of them walked home justified.
Luke introduces the parable with words so precise that we should not rush past them. In the Greek text, Jesus speaks to people described as:
τοὺς πεποιθότας ἐφ’ ἑαυτοῖς ὅτι εἰσὶν δίκαιοι
Tous pepoithotas eph’ heautois hoti eisin dikaioi.
They had become confident—trusting in themselves—that they were righteous.
But Luke adds something else:
καὶ ἐξουθενοῦντας τοὺς λοιπούς
...kai exouthenountas tous loipous.
And they treated the others with contempt.
That connection is devastating.
Confidence in personal righteousness had begun producing contempt for other people.
Jesus was not confronting atheists who mocked holiness.
He was confronting religious confidence.
Two men went to the temple to pray.
One was a Pharisee.
The other was a tax collector.
If you already know the story, resist the temptation to immediately make the Pharisee the villain.
That can become another form of the very sin Jesus is exposing.
“Thank God I am not like that Pharisee.”
Do you see how quickly the trap closes?
The Pharisee begins praying:
Ὁ θεός, εὐχαριστῶ σοι...
Ho Theos, eucharistō soi...
“God, I thank You...”
It sounds beautiful at first.
He addresses God.
He gives thanks.
Then comes the poison.
He is thankful that he is not like other people.
Not extortioners.
Not unjust people.
Not adulterers.
Then his eyes apparently find the man standing farther away.
“...or even like this tax collector.”
There it is.
A man standing before a holy God somehow manages to make another sinner the measuring stick of his righteousness.
And we still do it.
Maybe you no longer get drunk.
But now you despise the alcoholic.
Maybe God delivered you from sexual immorality.
But now you speak about sexually broken people as though disgust were a fruit of the Spirit.
Maybe your marriage survived.
But somewhere inside, you feel superior to the divorced believer sitting three rows behind you.

Maybe your children are walking with God, and instead of falling on your knees thanking Him for mercy, you quietly conclude that another parent's struggling child proves something about their parenting.
Maybe you know Scripture.
Maybe you understand doctrine.
Maybe you can spot theological error in thirty seconds.
But knowledge that should have driven you to worship has instead become ammunition for winning arguments and humiliating people.
Maybe you tithe.
Maybe you fast.
Maybe you serve.
Maybe you never miss Sunday worship.
Maybe you have been a Christian for thirty years.
And none of those things are evil.
That is precisely what makes self-righteousness so deceptive.
The Pharisee was not boasting about committing adultery.
He was boasting about religious obedience.
“I fast twice a week.”
“I give tithes of all that I get.”
The problem was not that fasting was evil.
The problem was not generosity.
The problem was not obedience.
The problem was where his confidence had landed.
His obedience had stopped being evidence of dependence upon God and had become evidence in the courtroom of his own imagination that he was better than somebody else.
This is one of the most dangerous transformations that can happen in a Christian life.
God rescues us from obvious sin...
and eventually we begin admiring the person He rescued.
We forget the pit.
We forget the chains.
We forget the nights when nobody knew what was happening inside us.
We forget how many prayers God answered that we did not deserve.
We forget how many temptations He prevented us from encountering.
We forget how many times grace restrained us.
We forget that if there is anything genuinely beautiful growing in our lives, God deserves the glory.
Then slowly...
mercy becomes résumé.
Testimony becomes trophy.
Conviction becomes comparison.
Holiness becomes hierarchy.
And the rescued sinner begins looking down into the pit at people who have not climbed out yet.
But perhaps the most frightening detail in Jesus' story is this:
The Pharisee was standing in the temple.
You can leave the nightclub and bring pride into the sanctuary.
You can throw away the bottle and keep the arrogance.
You can abandon pornography and become addicted to superiority.
You can stop swearing and begin murdering people with contempt.
You can leave worldly rebellion behind while carrying your self-righteousness straight through the church doors.
You can change your clothes without changing your confidence.
You can change your habits without changing your heart.
You can become respectable without becoming humble.
Then Jesus turns our attention toward the other man.
The tax collector stands far away.
He will not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He beats his chest.
No spiritual résumé.
No comparison.
No list of accomplishments.
No attempt to explain why somebody else is worse.
Just this:
Ὁ θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ.
Ho Theos, hilastheti moi tō hamartōlō.
“God, be merciful to me, the sinner.”
What a prayer.
He has stopped negotiating.
He has stopped comparing.
He has stopped pretending.
He brings God the one thing the Pharisee refuses to bring:
his need for mercy.
And Jesus says something that must have stunned His listeners.
The tax collector went home δεδικαιωμένος — dedikaiōmenos.
Justified.
Declared righteous before God.
Not because tax collecting made him righteous.
Not because sin suddenly became harmless.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Not because God lowered His standard.
He went home justified because he came before God without pretending that his righteousness could save him.
This is where the parable points us toward the beating heart of the Gospel.
Because the Christian message is not:
“Bad people should try harder until God likes them.”
It is not:
“Become slightly better than the person beside you.”
It is not:
“Clean yourself up enough and perhaps heaven will be impressed.”
The Gospel announces that sinners need a righteousness they cannot manufacture.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
The sinless Son of God lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
At the cross, He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And those who turn from sin and trust in Christ do not stand before God boasting, “Look what I achieved.”
We stand amazed and confess:
“Look what Jesus has done.”
That changes everything.
Because when the cross becomes enormous in your vision, superiority becomes absurd.
How can I kneel beneath a blood-stained cross where the innocent Son of God died for sinners...
and brag that my particular collection of sins looks more respectable than yours?
How can I sing about amazing grace on Sunday and treat someone as beneath me on Monday?
How can I rejoice that Christ did not reject me at my ugliest and then decide somebody else is too ugly for my compassion?
The cross does not tell me my sin was small.
The cross tells me my sin was so serious that Christ had to die—and His grace is so astonishing that He willingly came to save sinners.
That destroys both despair and pride.
The broken sinner cannot say, “I am beyond mercy.”
The religious sinner cannot say, “I am beyond needing mercy.”
Both must come to Jesus.
Perhaps this article is uncomfortable because you have genuinely changed.
You really did leave things behind.
You really did stop sleeping around.
You really did become sober.
You really did become faithful.
You really did begin reading Scripture.
You really did become disciplined.
Praise God.
Do not return to the chains Christ broke.
Do not romanticize your old bondage.
Do not confuse humility with pretending obedience does not matter.
Jesus calls us to repentance, holiness, faithfulness, love, obedience, and transformed lives.
But never forget Who gets the glory.
Christian maturity is not reaching a point where you need grace less.
Christian maturity is seeing more clearly how completely dependent upon Christ you have always been.
Maybe somebody entered church this morning smelling like cigarettes while you smelled like expensive perfume.
Maybe someone's marriage is collapsing while yours appears strong.
Maybe somebody has relapsed.
Maybe someone's teenager is rebelling.
Maybe somebody walked through the doors after committing a sin last night that would horrify you.
Maybe someone is sitting quietly while fighting an addiction nobody knows exists.
Maybe the person scrolling through Christian posts and never commenting is secretly wondering whether Jesus would still receive them if everyone knew the truth.
And perhaps the question heaven is pressing upon us is not merely:
“What did they do?”
Perhaps it is:
“Have you forgotten what mercy did for you?”
There is a difference between discernment and contempt.
Biblical Christianity does not require us to call evil good.
Jesus never needed to redefine sin in order to love sinners.
Truth and mercy met perfectly in Him.
We can call people to repentance without treating ourselves as their savior.
We can oppose sin without despising sinners.
We can pursue holiness without converting holiness into a pedestal.
We can defend truth without forgetting that truth revealed our own guilt before it ever became something we used to correct somebody else.
And perhaps one of the clearest signs that grace has gone deep is that obedience makes us more grateful, not more arrogant.
The closer we walk with Jesus, the less impressive our spiritual résumé begins to look beside His holiness.
Suddenly the prayer changes.
Not:
“God, thank You that I am better than them.”
But:
“Jesus, thank You that You did not abandon me.”
“Jesus, keep my heart tender.”
“Jesus, expose whatever pride is hiding beneath my obedience.”
“Jesus, teach me to hate sin without learning to hate sinners.”
“Jesus, if I become more holy, make me more humble too.”
Somebody reading this has spent years trying to become “the good Christian.”
You have become dependable.
Disciplined.
Respected.
People ask you for advice.
People assume your spiritual life is strong.
And perhaps somewhere underneath all of that goodness is an exhausted soul constantly measuring itself against everyone else.
Better than him.
More faithful than her.
More biblical than them.
More disciplined.
More conservative.
More generous.
More committed.
More spiritual.
And Jesus is offering you freedom from that prison too.
You do not have to be the best person in the room.
You need Christ.
You do not have to prove somebody else is worse in order to believe God loves you.
You need Christ.
You do not need another person's failure to validate your obedience.
You need Christ.
You do not need to hide your weakness beneath religious achievement.
You need Christ.
And when Christ becomes your righteousness rather than merely the mascot attached to your righteousness, something beautiful happens.
You can finally look at the struggling sinner without needing to stand above them.
You can kneel beside them.
You can say:
“I know where mercy is.”
That is Christianity.
Not one beggar bragging to another beggar about having cleaner clothes.
It is one rescued sinner pointing another toward the Savior.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.

Not to create an audience of Christians who congratulate themselves for knowing more than everyone else, but to keep pointing wounded, growing, repenting people back toward Jesus Christ, Scripture, grace, truth, holiness, restoration, and the Gospel.
If this exposed something uncomfortable in you, don't rush past it.
Be honest before God.
Not as a performance.
Not to prove spirituality.
Let it be a small public confession that none of us graduates from needing grace.
There may be another believer reading those words who needs to know they are not the only one still being sanctified.
Then think of one person you love.
Not somebody you want to insult.
Not somebody you want to “teach a lesson.”
Someone you genuinely love.
Come back to it the next time another person's failure begins making you feel spiritually tall.
It doesn't.
Not because financial support proves you are a better Christian.
It doesn't.
And certainly not because grace can be purchased.
It cannot.
Jesus purchased redemption at a price none of us could pay.
But Christians can freely choose to glorify God through generosity, stewardship, sharing biblical truth, and helping sound Gospel ministry reach more people.
Think about Jesus.
Think about the temple.
Think about those two men.
One had an impressive résumé.
The other had a desperate prayer.
One looked across the room and saw someone beneath him.
The other looked toward heaven and knew mercy was his only hope.
And Jesus said the second man went home justified.
So tonight, before you tell God everything you have done right...
before you remember everything somebody else has done wrong...
before you congratulate yourself for how far you have come...
remember the tax collector standing far away.
Remember his lowered eyes.
Remember his hand striking his chest.
Remember his prayer.
Ὁ θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ.
God...
have mercy on me,
the sinner.
Perhaps the greatest evidence that Jesus has changed you is not that you can finally see how sinful everyone else is.
Perhaps it is that after everything He has changed in you, you are still astonished that He had mercy on you.
And here is the line I hope follows you long after you close this article:
Be careful that the sins you conquered do not become the throne from which you judge the sinners Jesus died to save.
Because the scandal was never too ugly for His grace.
The sinner was never too dirty for His mercy.
And the religious heart was never too respectable to need repentance.
